column3: What qualities matter most to you in a civic technology project?

For me it comes down to whether a project is genuinely open — open source code, open data, and open governance. I'm sceptical of civic tech that's built by well-meaning organisations but remains a black box. If communities can't inspect, adapt, or fork it, it's not really theirs. I also care a lot about whether the people most affected by a problem were involved in designing the solution.

I work in local government so I think about scalability and interoperability constantly. The projects that excite me are ones that have figured out how to plug into existing systems rather than asking councils to replace everything. Open standards matter more to me than open source — a well-documented API that any supplier can implement is often more impactful than a beautifully written codebase nobody deploys.

Accountability and transparency are my north stars. We have so much civic tech that helps governments communicate outward but very little that helps citizens hold power to account. I want to see projects that make it harder for bad actors to hide — whether that's corporate misconduct, parliamentary doublespeak, or opaque decision-making in public bodies.

I'm most excited by projects that work at the grassroots level — tools built with and for communities that wouldn't otherwise have a voice in political processes. Global reach is nice but I'd rather see something deeply embedded in one place and genuinely used than something deployed everywhere and trusted nowhere. Participation and co-design matter enormously to me.

My background is in deliberative democracy so I care deeply about whether a tool actually changes how decisions get made, not just whether it collects opinions. There's a lot of civic tech that creates the appearance of consultation without any meaningful feedback loop. I want to see projects where you can draw a clear line between the tool and a real change in policy or resource allocation.

Honestly, deployment scale and real-world uptake matter most to me. Ideas are cheap — the hard part is getting institutions to actually use something. I'm impressed by projects that have navigated the procurement and change management challenges of working with government, even if the underlying technology is relatively simple. Proven adoption over elegant prototypes.

I think about the global south a lot. Most civic tech is built for wealthy democracies with high digital literacy and reliable internet. The projects I find most compelling are ones designed to work under constrained conditions — low bandwidth, feature phones, multilingual — or that have been genuinely adapted and adopted outside their country of origin.

Election integrity and voter participation are my focus. I want to see projects that make it easier for people to engage with democratic processes — registering, understanding candidates, finding polling stations, tracking results. The boring infrastructure of democracy is underinvested and underappreciated. I'm less excited by flashy deliberation tools and more by the unglamorous data pipelines that make everything else possible.
